This study introduces the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with Exogenous Covariates (TV-PARX) model, a flexible framework designed to capture nonlinear dynamics, structural breaks, and time-varying covariate effects in count data. We establish the global asymptotic consistency of the least squares estimator under general mixing conditions and specific moment requirements. Furthermore, we derive local asymptotic normality for the TV-PARX model when covariates are bounded, assuming a positive definite Hessian matrix. These theoretical findings are validated through simulations and an empirical analysis of daily Twitter volume regarding the COVID-19 pandemic. The results demonstrate that the TV-PARX model effectively identifies structural breaks and nonlinear patterns in the data. To facilitate practical implementation, we develop an R package available at https://github.com/chenyuxia/TVPARX.

This study presents a novel method for monitoring the vertical aerosol optical depth ($\tau_{\rm A}$) in real-time, independent of source brightness, using wide-field photometry of the sky dome. While optical extinction measurements between source and detector offer high precision, they require stable, well-calibrated instruments and bright, variable sources. In contrast, the technique described here exploits atmospheric scattering to establish an absolute scale. Although this approach yields lower precision than optical extinction methods, it provides a crucial absolute reference. When combined with high-precision relative optical extinction data, it enables the derivation of precise $\tau_{\rm A}$ values without needing prior absolute calibration. We demonstrate the feasibility of this method through a four-month dataset from the 10-metre Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (VLA) at Socorro, New Mexico, utilizing a simple, fully automated system. The results from this site align well with concurrent readings from a Sun photometer and a lidar. Furthermore, we show that this method can be implemented with minimal hardware and is easily adaptable to other radio telescope sites. Given its simplicity, low cost, and fully automated nature, this technique has the potential to become a standard practice for large, multi-meter astronomical sites. By leveraging existing optical monitoring systems, it can help ensure that radio telescope time is utilized during periods of clear atmospheric conditions. Our analysis indicates that, on average, the VLA's wide-field optical monitoring system underestimates $\tau_{\rm A}$ by approximately 0.01–0.02 compared to the simple scattering model employed here; future work will focus on refining this model to enhance accuracy. To access the raw data supporting this study, visit: https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020arXiv200610063M/abstract. Our findings suggest that large astronomical sites can adopt this simple, low-cost, automated method to optimize the use of radio telescope time, ensuring access during periods of optimal atmospheric clarity. By utilizing current optical monitoring infrastructure, this approach can complement existing systems like Sun photometers and lidars at radio telescope locations. We hope this method encourages the adoption of simple, low-cost, automated solutions at major astronomical sites to maximize radio telescope time usage during periods of best atmospheric visibility. This study compares the computational efficiency and accuracy of three numerical methods—Car-Parrinello molecular dynamics (CPMD), ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD), and geometry optimization (GO)—for simulating a small biomolecular system, the alanine dipeptide. By employing a mixed strategy that runs GO and AIMD in parallel, we evaluated the impact of different GO time steps ($dt_{GO}$) on both accuracy and efficiency. The simulations employed density functional theory (DFT) using the PBE functional with the CPMD package. Our results indicate that extending the GO time step significantly reduces overall simulation time without compromising sampling quality, as measured by the potential energy autocorrelation function. Specifically, increasing $dt_{GO}$ from 0.05 to 0.2 fs yielded a nine-fold reduction in total runtime with negligible loss in accuracy. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the "fidelity" of the AIMD approximation relative to DFT-GO is a more critical factor for simulation efficiency than the specific AIMD time step. These conclusions are supported by a simple harmonic oscillator model, which offers general guidelines for optimizing CPMD and AIMD simulations of small molecular systems. Ultimately, this mixed GO-AIMD approach enables longer sampling durations, thereby enhancing conformational sampling in small molecules and potentially facilitating the investigation of electronic structure effects in larger molecular systems. To facilitate replication, the input files and output logs for all simulations are accessible at https://github.

Although recent years have seen substantial progress in image captioning systems, the evaluation metrics used to assess these models remain problematic. These flawed metrics hinder the development of high-quality image description guidelines that are user-centric, especially for visually impaired individuals who rely on such systems. Furthermore, existing guidelines are often derived from meta-discussions about model performance rather than the actual experiences of end-users, and they lack specific recommendations for optimizing descriptions for particular use cases. Consequently, there is an urgent need to establish more robust guidelines grounded in the real-world requirements of visually impaired users. This paper introduces a comprehensive framework for creating image description guidelines, detailing each step of the process with an emphasis on ensuring user-centricity. We demonstrate this framework by developing guidelines for two distinct tasks: optimizing descriptions for lower-quality images and for users with varying levels of visual acuity. Although developed specifically for visually impaired users, this framework is adaptable and can be applied to create guidelines for a wide range of applications. Additionally, we release a dataset containing guidelines for two tasks designed for blind users in India, which will be made publicly available.

The optimization of renormalization scale choices constitutes a significant challenge in quantum field theory, which can be formulated as an Euler-Arnold gradient descent problem. By leveraging the Euler-Arnold equation, we derive a system of linear differential equations with respect to the logarithm of the renormalization scale. Solving this system via a power series expansion in the ultraviolet cutoff yields a polynomial expression for the beta function dependent on the logarithm of the cutoff and the anomalous dimensions of operator insertions. We apply this methodology to $O(N)$ scalar field theory in four dimensions, focusing on the four-point function. Utilizing a recently developed perturbative framework for calculating nonlocal gauge-invariant operators, we determine the polynomial form of the beta function by solving a linear system involving anomalous dimensions. As an application, we graphically illustrate the gradient descent of the effective coupling constant across the two-point correlation length, demonstrating the approach's clarity and efficacy. Finally, we extend this method to derive the polynomial expression for the gamma function and propose a similar graphical representation for the convex G function. To facilitate these applications, we also provide an open-source Python package designed to solve the linear systems required for finding the polynomial beta function and to support further applications. Our results confirm the robustness of this method as a practical tool for extending calculations deep into the UV cutoff regime. Furthermore, the derived polynomial beta function offers a valuable resource for exploring scale invariant points in the phase diagram and determining critical exponents within the Euclidean framework through Monte Carlo simulations. Among the utility features of this package, we also derive the polynomial expression for the causal spectral density, which had previously remained undocumented. To maximize the method's effectiveness, we derive the polynomial beta function as closely to the UV cutoff as computationally feasible; consequently, we present the results for $S^3$ and $\mathbb{R}^3$ (where the UV cutoff is limited by the maximal feasible loop order), and for a set of theoretical UV cutoff values at higher loop orders to guide future computational efforts. At non-zero temperature and baryon chemical potential, QCD exhibits confinement alongside a transition to a deconfined quark-gluon plasma. Within this regime, quarks and gluons experience significant interactions mediated by the exchange of heavy quark-antiquark pairs, commonly known as "mesons." Because these masses exceed the typical thermal energy scale, such exchanges can be modeled as static sources. Consequently, the forces between heavy quarks and between heavy mesons serve as a crucial probe of the underlying QCD medium. In this work, we examine the in-medium modifications of the spin-dependent potential between two static charm quarks ($D$) and between charmonia ($\chi_Q$) using two distinct approaches. Initially, we derive the in-medium spectral density of the gluon exchange connecting the heavy quarks from the QCD medium's spectral action. Subsequently, we solve the Bethe-Salpeter equation to determine the binding energy of the heavy quark-antiquark pair as a function of temperature. Our findings indicate that the spectral density of the exchanged gluon—and consequently the force between the heavy quarks—remains largely unchanged by the medium at distances where the inter-quark potential is linear. This contrasts with previous expectations of significant medium-induced suppression in the gluon spectrum at short separations, a consequence of our derived spectral density not vanishing for spacelike momenta. These results imply that in-medium changes in the heavy quark-antiquark potential arise from alterations at large separations, where the medium influences the dynamics of the pair itself. Our derived spectral density and the resulting binding energy align well with recent lattice QCD data. As an additional application, we analyze the melting temperature of $D\bar{D}$ mesons and various charmonia and bottomonia states. Furthermore, we estimate the suppression of $\chi_Q\bar{\chi}_Q$ production in heavy ion collisions, finding that this suppression is more pronounced than previously anticipated.

This study introduces a wideband waveforming optimization framework designed to enhance the fair-throughput of user equipments (UEs) with potentially non-overlapping wideband allocated resources. The system model accounts for the coexistence of narrowband and wideband communications, where UEs are served via either method. Furthermore, the model incorporates inter- and intractual interference resulting from wideband waveforming, as well as mutual interference between narrowband and wideband signals. Focusing on an OFDM-based narrowband communication scheme and a single-contiguous wideband waveform, the problem of optimizing either fair-throughput or sum-throughput is formulated as a mixed integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) challenge. An efficient alternating optimization algorithm is proposed to solve this MINLP, guaranteeing convergence to a locally optimal solution. Fuzzy logic is employed to identify the optimal wideband waveform, which may be either single-contiguous or multi-contiguous. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the proposed wideband waveforming strategy significantly increases both fair-throughput and sum-throughput compared to conventional methods. Additionally, the results indicate that the fuzzy logic-based approach for selecting the wideband waveform yields superior fair-throughput performance than restricting systems to a single-contiguous waveform. The system model and simulations were conducted in a 5G New Radio (NR) environment, with a total wideband of 400 MHz and narrowband communications operating across 20 carrier frequencies. Focusing on intractual interference, the simulations assumed no guard bands between subbands, while the optimization process selected a single-contiguous wideband waveform. Future research could explore multi-contiguous waveforms and address intertractual interference caused by out-of-band emissions. Additionally, the simulations utilized a linear antenna array for both narrowband and wideband communications; future work could investigate single-point source wideband waveforms, similar to those used in 4G LTE systems. Finally, while this paper concentrates on a point-to-point communication scenario, extending the system model and optimization strategies to point-to-multipoint scenarios is a promising direction for future study. By signally allocating narrowband resources to UEs with poor channel conditions and wideband resources to those with favorable conditions, this research offers a practical solution for heterogeneous narrowband-wideband systems. Such allocation strategies are applicable in various scenarios, including public safety communications, where different groups may operate on narrowband and wideband channels, and in commercial deployments involving legacy devices and new high-data-rate users. This study presents a global fitting methodology for Parton Distribution Functions (PDFs), grounded in a neural network-based parameterization across both $x$ and $Q^2$ variables. The fitting procedure relies on a least-square minimization of a $\chi^2$ function, which incorporates experimental uncertainties and inter-dependent errors among data points at varying $Q^2$ levels via the DGLAP evolution operator. We demonstrate that the dynamics of the DGLAP operator at $Q^2$ scales of 5 GeV and below significantly influence the fitting process. The resulting fitted PDFs are compared against the CT14, MMHT14, and ABMP13 sets. Our findings indicate that our approach yields a smooth $Q^2$ dependence for the fitted PDFs, with quality comparable to standard non-parametric grids. Furthermore, the fitted parameters exhibit strong correlations with those of existing PDF sets, suggesting that this global fitting method on a neural network grid is a viable technique for exploring new PDF sets. The source files for this study are accessible at https://github.com/huynhtuan2001/Neuro-PDF. To investigate acoustic instabilities, two flamelet models—the linearized steady-state flamelet model and the linearized flamelet-generated progress variable (FL-CPV) model—were developed and compared. Results indicate that the FL-CPV model offers superior accuracy, particularly in regions with elevated acoustic fluctuations. Consequently, the FL-CPV model is recommended for linearized analyses of turbulent reacting flows, while the linearized steady-state flamelet model remains suitable for cases where acoustic fluctuations are minimal. Furthermore, an instability mechanism was identified analogous to that in shear-driven jets: the Kelvin-Helmholtz (KH) instability amplifies turbulent fluctuations, which in turn intensify acoustic waves, creating a feedback loop. However, no self-excited mode was observed in the current configuration, as the necessary positive feedback loop was absent. Finally, it is concluded that increasing the equivalence ratio would likely trigger acoustic instabilities by enhancing thermo-acoustic feedback. These findings were obtained via LES, and future research should explore this configuration using DNS. Among various linearized turbulence-reaction closure models assessed, the Eulerian filtered-variable flamelet model with an unactivated chaotic-puff activation function ($\Lambda_{FFP}=0$) performed optimally within the linearized framework. Consequently, this model was selected for the current analysis. A linearized acoustic boundary condition was imposed at the inlet pipe lid to excite instabilities, implemented through a superposition of global modes determined via a shooting method applied to the linearized governing equations. The phenomenon of strangeness enhancement in multi-parton systems has been a central topic of research at the LHC and RHIC. While this effect has been extensively documented when comparing proton-lead (p-Pb) or heavy-ion (A-A) collisions to proton-proton (p-p) baselines, the specific origin of this enhancement in p-p interactions remains unclear. In this study, we present an updated analysis of charm and strange hadron production across a wide range of multiplicities in $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV p-p collisions using the ATLAS detector. By normalizing production yields to the inelastic cross-section, we observe that the per-yield of both charm and strange hadrons increases with multiplicity and aligns with the scaling expected for A-A systems. Furthermore, when these yields are expressed per binary collision, the p-p data at $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV fall between the scaled A-A yields at 2.76 TeV and 5 TeV. These findings indicate that the "suppression" of strange and charm hadron yields per binary collision in low-multiplicity p-p collisions is not due to the absence of multi-parton interactions, but rather results from non-linear gluon saturation and/or the formation of a "glueball" state at high parton densities. At lower densities, hadron production in p-p is best described by linear parton-to-hadron fragmentation. Conversely, at high densities, the production mechanism in both p-p and A-A systems is governed by parton coalescence or "recombination." This transition from fragmentation to coalescence at high densities offers a plausible explanation for strangeness enhancement in both p-p and A-A systems. Given that this effect is driven by parton density rather than system size, it is expected to occur in small systems at ultra-high energies, such as in proton-nucleus collisions at the future FCC-hh. Additionally, this transition provides a valuable probe for understanding parton dynamics in the initial state of heavy-ion collisions. Our conclusions are based on the assumption that soft hadron production at high multiplicities in p-p originates from hard parton interactions. The existence of a neutron star low-mass X-ray binary (NS-LMXB) with a specific accretion luminosity $L_a$ and spin period $P_c$ is not guaranteed for all Galactic NS-LMXBs. To identify those most likely to become millisecond radio pulsars (MSP-LMs), we introduce a "spin-up zone" on the $L_a$-$P_c$ diagram, defining the parameter range required for an companion star to fill its Roche lobe and enable accretion onto the neutron star. Applying this framework to the known Galactic MSP population, we estimate that approximately 3000 -6000+2000 millisecond LMXBs should evolve from current NS-LMXBs and potentially be detected as radio pulsars once they have spent $10^8$ - $10^9$ years in an low-mass binary system. This estimate aligns well with the observed millisecond radio pulsar population in the Galaxy. We also examine the prospects for identifying these systems among the upcoming catalog of thousands of newly discovered millisecond pulsars from the SKA-LOW survey. Additionally, we briefly assess the prospects for finding similar binaries in the Milky Way's bulge and halo, as well as in other galaxies. Our analysis confirms that the transition from an NS-LMXB to an MSP-LMXB is a rare event, dependent on specific initial conditions, which helps explain why multi-male MSP-LMs have been identified in other galaxies but remain undetected in the local group. Our findings also offer guidance for interpreting the non-detection of an MSP-LMXB in the gravitational wave source GW190814. Ultimately, this study provides a comprehensive overview of the lifecycle of NS-LMXBs and their evolution into MSP-LMs. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/chenyux1993/Spin_Up_Zone.

Complementing these results, we prove that splliting vertices is sufficient to attain planarity for any bipartite graph that admits an optimal embedding. Finally, we present an algorithm capable of finding the graph with the minimal number of splits that is renderable via an optimized non-planar visualization; however, this approach runs in $O(n^{2.72})$ time. To enable this optimization, we first define a set of geometric constraints required for renderability, then verify 2.5D embeddability against these constraints using linear-space linear-time techniques originally developed for 3D point set surface rendering. As a side outcome, this verification process also generates a specific layout for the graph. This study introduces HyperDegrade, a new side-channel attack designed to surpass the efficacy of Flush+Reload (F&R) and its variants in both time granularity and the feasibility of remote implementation. HyperDegrade combines cache eviction with a remote processor degradation technique called HyperSleep, which utilizes the CPUID instruction to trigger deep C-states during the eviction phase. Unlike F&R, which relies on measuring execution time differences between normal and eviction operations, HyperDegrade evaluates how well the eviction operation degrades execution time compared to a baseline of repeated baselines. We demonstrate that HyperSleep causes Intel and AMD processors to enter deeper C-states than previously known, increasing execution time gaps by a factor of three to four over baseline executions. In controlled environments, HyperDegrade achieves time granularity 10x better than Flush+Reload (reaching 1.7 microseconds) and requires 50% fewer traces to identify target operations. These results indicate that HyperDegrade offers superior efficacy to Flush+Reload in targeted settings. To assess feasibility in remote scenarios, we developed a noise model accounting for execution time variations caused by physical and virtual context switches. Our findings suggest that HyperDegrade remains viable even with as few as 20 traces under noisy conditions. Based on these noise characteristics, we constructed a cryptographic key extraction attack using Bitcoin wallet operations. This attack successfully derived the correct private key with a 93% success rate using 100 execution traces, outperforming the best existing remote side-channel key extraction methods. To further enhance efficacy and address the feasibility of remote exploitation, we developed an optimized variant, HyperDegrade+, which utilizes a new baseline operation to maximize execution time gaps. While this improvement increases the executions needed per trace, it remains more effective than HyperDegrade in controlled environments and likely feasible in remote scenarios given sufficient traces per point of interest. We validated HyperDegrade+ in a simulated attack chain, achieving superior time granularity and lower trace requirements for identifying target operations. In this demonstration, a remote entity first executed HyperDegrade+ within a attack library, followed by Stuff&Dump to extract memory contents, ultimately succeeding in deriving the private key from an encrypted wallet— a feat previously unachievable in a remote setting. To mitigate these threats, we recommend OS-level countermeasures similar to those used to defend against Flush+Reload, specifically ensuring that eviction operations do not induce processor sleep states. However, implementing this defense against HyperDegrade is more challenging than for F&R variants

We introduce a new class of moves, termed diagonal moves, applicable to $n$-bridge braids and braid diagrams. It is demonstrated that two braid words are equivalent under regular isotopy if and only if they are equivalent via a combination of twisting, crossing changes, and diagonal moves. Furthermore, an explicit formula is provided to convert between diagonal moves and the composite action of twisting plus a crossing change. These moves are also extended to knotted strings and torus knots, where it is shown that any two torus knots differing only in the number of diagonal moves are related through a sequence of twisting, crossing changes, and diagonal moves. Finally, the concept of diagonal moves is generalized to braided manifolds, and an explicit formula is derived for this broader context. The utility of diagonal moves is further illustrated by providing an alternative proof that the symplectic crossing number of a non-trivial torus knot $T(2,n)$ ($n\geq 3$) equals its twisting number plus two, and by establishing a lower bound for the symplectic self-intersection number of knotted strings within four-dimensional symplectic manifolds. Finally, a conjecture regarding the equivalence of two braid words under diagonal moves and their stabilization is presented. These moves offer an efficient method for transforming knotted structures while preserving specific topological characteristics. Our approach finds applications in topology, knot theory, quantum field theory, chemistry, and DNA research. Potential uses in coding theory and cryptography are also discussed. This study investigates how the distribution of task difficulties influences the decision-making strategies of multi-agent systems in a simple grid world. We employ a contextual linear Thompson sampling algorithm to learn optimal action-context pairings, with the context defined by local agent densities. Our findings indicate that when tasks are uniformly distributed, agents in under-resourced contexts tend to adopt exploitation strategies, whereas those in over-resourced contexts favor exploration. Conversely, when tasks follow a power-law distribution characterized by high variability, exploitation becomes dominant in well-resourced contexts while under-resourced contexts shift toward exploration. These results align with the "common sense" of local majority exploitation under uniform distributions and switching strategies when tasks are power-law distributed. To validate these conclusions, we conducted experiments in both static and dynamic environments, as well as in settings with varying levels of contextual sparsity. Ultimately, our approach to contextual learning outperforms non-contextual baseline methods across all tested environments. Our work underscores the significance of contextual information in multi-agent systems and offers actionable insights for designing and deploying such systems in real-world applications.

Regarding the context of our research, the concept of "common sense" is not fixed but rather contingent upon the specific environment and problem at hand. For instance, in a fire rescue scenario, the common sense strategy would involve prioritizing tasks based on urgency and difficulty rather than a uniform distribution. Similarly, in a search and rescue operation, agents would focus on areas with the highest probability of locating a victim. These examples illustrate that task distributions are typically non-uniform and often follow power-law distributions. Consequently, our goal is to develop a learning algorithm capable of adapting to different task distributions, whether uniform or power-law. This study examines the Cartesian Product $A\times A$ of a finite set $A$ equipped with two potentially distinct unary operations, forming the foundation for Cartesian Decomposition. The analysis centers on the stabilizer subgroup $G_{(x,y)}$ associated with each pair $(x,y)\in A\times A$. We investigate the regularity of the action of the Cartesian Decomposition on $A\times A$ and its relationship with the regularity of the group actions of $G_{(x,y)}$ on $A$. Furthermore, we establish a characterization of diagonal groups within the context of Cartesian Decomposition and provide a constructive algorithm for this decomposition. Finally, we apply these concepts to define an operator that increases the rank of a function on $A\times 2$. As an application, we present an improved upper bound for Tseitin contradictions on a binary tree graph, demonstrating that $\mathsf{R}(\mathcal{P})\leq |\mathcal{P}|+3$. Our results are illustrated through specific examples and visualized using the free software package for Cartesian Product analysis available at \url{http://www.math.auckland.ac.nz/~gkpa/cartprod/}.

Sloshing-Sagnac interferometers represent a topological modification of conventional interferometer architectures, offering an additional degree of freedom that potentially enhances sensitivity to signal strains. This study employs a sloshing-Sagnac configuration to create squeezed-light sources for both forward- and backward-propagating waves, which are then integrated into the arm sections of a Michelson interferometer. We theoretically examine the sloshing-Sagnac topology and derive its optimal squeezing angle, subsequently modeling a Michelson interferometer equipped with this dual-probing sloshing-Sagnac setup. Under the Wigner-Cayley-Ket formalism, we numerically optimize the sloshing-Sagnac geometry and the squeezing amplitude and direction to maximize signal-srand responsiveness. Compared to a standard Michelson setup using a single squeezed-light source, this dual-probing arrangement demonstrates improved signal-srand folding characteristics, yielding 1.5 dB greater effective sensitivity at frequencies of 100 Hz and below. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved significant success in automatically identifying regions of interest in medical images for diagnostic support. This paper introduces a data augmentation strategy designed to effectively utilize convolutional neural networks for segmentation tasks with limited medical image data. We evaluate this approach using the public dataset of left ventricular and myocardial infarction segments, known as the ACDC dataset. Our method combines image rotation with a random cropping technique that preserves the corresponding label information. The resulting augmented dataset is then employed to train a U-Net architecture. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing techniques across all standard segmentation metrics when working with small datasets. Furthermore, the approach shows no degradation in performance on larger datasets. These findings indicate that our strategy is effective for both small and large datasets. This study introduces a hybrid framework for 3D point cloud classification that integrates unsupervised and supervised feature extraction. Furthermore, the unsupervised feature extraction based on Inception-I metrics yields closer cluster centers to class centroids compared to other methods. Knowledge graphs (KGs) are structured data representations that have recently attracted significant attention for factual tasks, including the development of natural language processing models on knowledge graph-based datasets. In this work, we investigate the impact of pre-training models on factual triples derived from text-based knowledge graphs. Furthermore, when compared to GNN-based methods, our approach yields competitive results for the FQA task but underperforms in the Rec task. To support future research, we have made both the GQA-Rec and GRecRec datasets, along with our code, publicly available at https://github.com/GNNRec/GQA-Rec.

This paper addresses the concepts of invariance and decomposition of linear systems featuring variable coefficients and fractional-order derivatives. While invariance is a fundamental idea, defining it precisely for fractional systems is challenging due to the non-causal nature of these systems, which relies on an initial history function. We examine two distinct definitions of invariant subspaces: one requiring invariance for all admissible initial histories, and another focusing on systems starting from finite initial states. Analyzing the implications of these definitions, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for linear subspaces to remain invariant. Furthermore, we derive the invariant subspace decomposition theorem and provide explicit formulas for the component projections within the decomposition. Finally, we apply these results to determine the normal form of linear systems with a fixed integer order.

Leveraging Carleman estimates, we establish that both the observability inequality and the initial stability result governing the boundary observability of the biharmonic operator in an open subset of the boundary, can be upgraded to earn backward-in-time uniqueness of solutions. Finally, we highlight how this uniqueness result extends to the identification of the boundary regularizing operator in the forward model. As a byproduct, we derive a new observability inequality for the heat equation on a general domain, relying solely on boundary observations within a non-empty, open, and bounded subset of the boundary. At low energies, the dark sector can be described by a set of "dark mesons" arising from the spontaneous breaking of dark parity symmetry by a scalar condensate within a minimal dark sector. This symmetry remains approximately conserved due to the heaviness of the mediators responsible for generating dark meson masses. We extend a recent two-loop renormalization group analysis of an extended standard model to include this non-linearly realized dark meson sector. Our results indicate that vacuum stability and unitarity within this framework are sensitive to the mass of the additional scalar singlet required for seesaw mechanism consistency. Specifically, for type-I and type-II mechanisms, the singlet mass must be at least as heavy as the mediators. In contrast, type-III and see-saw-see-saw mechanisms allow for mediators that are heavier than the singlet. Furthermore, we observe that the preferred mass scale for these mediators is lower than previously anticipated, potentially falling within the reach of current and upcoming experiments. Finally, we demonstrate that the decay of the lightest dark meson into two singtons serves as a viable candidate for explaining the anomalous magnetic moment of the dark photon. Additionally, if the mediators are scalars, we show that a "hierarchy of mediators"—where vector mediators are significantly heavier than scalar mediators—is necessary to satisfy cosmological and astrophysical constraints. 

Notably, this study represents the first examination of a conformal vector mediator coupled to a non-linearly symmetric dark meson sector, whereas all prior investigations featured vector mediators as the sole new physics element. In those earlier models, the heavy vector mediators effectively replaced the non-linear symmetry breaking term, thereby masking the dark mesons. However, when vector mediators are made sufficiently heavy relative to the scalar mediators, the Weyl-invariant conformal vector sector decouples, leaving behind the non-linearly symmetric dark meson sector as the effective low-energy description. This allows for a consistent model featuring both vector and vector-like mediators operating at distinct mass scales. Our analysis confirms that such a multi-scale structure is viable and can remain stable and unitary up to high energy scales, provided the mediators are appropriately heavy and the vacuum alignment is correctly tuned.
